openers.strategic-interaction-and-game-theory: In every situation in this chapter, what is best for one player depends on what the others do. Game theory gives each player a strategy, a complete plan for every situation, and lays games out either as a table of payoffs or as a tree of moves. Some games are pure contests, where one side's gain is exactly the other's loss; others reward players who make the same choice, or who trust each other enough to aim high together. A central idea is the resting point where no one could do better by changing only their own choice. The chapter also follows what happens when the same game is played over and over, and how people split a surplus they can only create together, from bargaining tables to auctions.

nature-econ-731.title: Strategy: a complete plan for every situation
nature-econ-731.text: In game theory, a strategy is more than a move. It is a player's complete plan for a game, saying what they will do in every situation that might arise. A move, or action, is any single option a player can choose when the best result depends on what others do too. A strategy is like a list of directions, and a move is one step on that list. A player's strategy set lists every strategy open to them; in rock, paper, scissors it is {rock, paper, scissors}. In games played over time, or with private information, strategies become rules for responding to each possible history or piece of information. Choosing the strategy sets well is part of the art of making an applied game both solvable and meaningful.

nature-econ-671.title: Auctions: letting the highest bidder set the price
nature-econ-671.text: Each year the US EPA auctions about 250,000 allowances to the highest bidders, each letting its owner emit one ton of sulfur dioxide. An auction is a way of buying or selling by inviting bids and then dealing with the highest bidder, or, when buying, the lowest. The open ascending-price auction, where each bid must beat the one before, is probably the most common kind and has a long history. Auctions trade antiques, livestock, radio spectrum, used cars, real estate, online advertising and emission permits, among much else. Governments earn the most from spectrum and quota auctions: Russia's crab quota sold for €2 billion in 2019. Fishing quotas can be handed out free or auctioned when a catch-share scheme starts. The branch of economics that studies how auctions are designed and how bidders behave is auction theory. Paul Milgrom and Robert B. Wilson won the 2020 Nobel Prize for introducing new kinds of auction.

nature-econ-742.title: Zero-sum games: one side's gain is the other's loss
nature-econ-742.text: Cut a cake among people who value every piece equally, and a bigger slice for one leaves less for the rest. That is a zero-sum situation: one side's gain is exactly the other side's loss, so gains and losses add up to zero. Poker, chess, sport and bridge are everyday examples, and in finance so are futures, options and swaps. Such games are distributive. Good negotiation cannot enlarge the pie, only divide it. They are also unusually tidy to solve. Every two-player finite zero-sum game has an equilibrium once players may randomize. There, the {{ref:nature-econ-718}} and the older minimax and maximin rules all give the same answer, which can be found with {{ref:nature-econ-456}}. In 1944 von Neumann and Morgenstern went further. They showed that any game of n players, even one whose gains and losses need not cancel, equals a zero-sum game with an extra fictitious player.

nature-econ-687.title: Cooperative bargaining: splitting a surplus made together
nature-econ-687.text: A firm and its workers must split a profit; two trading partners must set their terms of trade. Each pair faces the problem of cooperative bargaining: how to divide a surplus they can only create together. Because the surplus can be divided many ways, they must negotiate. A bargaining problem has two parts: the set of feasible agreements, and a {{ref:nature-econ-688}} giving each side's payoff if no deal is reached. Economists approach it in two ways. The normative approach sets out appealing rules, called axioms, that a fair division should satisfy. The positive approach studies how surpluses are actually shared, modelling bargaining as a non-cooperative game, most often with offers made in sequence. Experiments found no consistent support for any model; many people settled on simple solutions good for both sides. Kenneth Binmore used the Nash bargaining game and {{ref:nature-econ-707}} to explain why people see a 50–50 split as the just solution.

nature-econ-722.title: The normal form: a game laid out as a table
nature-econ-722.text: The simplest picture of a game is a table. In the normal form, or payoff matrix, the rows list one player's possible strategies and the columns the other's. Each cell gives the row player's payoff first and the column player's second. The format suits games where players move at the same time, or cannot see each other's move first. It makes strategies that are always beaten easy to spot, along with stable outcomes. In the prisoner's dilemma matrix, Defect beats Cooperate whatever the other does, so (Defect, Defect) is the only {{ref:nature-econ-718}}. The table does lose some information compared with a game tree. A game played in turns fits a table only if every contingent plan is listed, even for situations that never arise. Every tree has an equivalent table, but converting can make the representation exponentially larger.

nature-econ-718.title: Nash equilibrium: where no one gains by moving alone
nature-econ-718.text: Each traveller's journey time depends on the routes everyone else picks. Predicting traffic therefore means predicting how all those choices settle together. That is the job of the Nash equilibrium. It is a situation in a game where no player could do better by changing only their own strategy, while everyone else keeps theirs. It applies to any strategic interaction, where each decision-maker's outcome depends on the others' choices as well as their own. Nash's insight was that the choices of several decision-makers cannot be predicted by analysing each one in isolation. The idea is named after John Forbes Nash Jr., but Antoine Augustin Cournot used the same reasoning in 1838 for firms choosing how much to produce. A Nash equilibrium is stable, not necessarily good. It need not be Pareto optimal, so it can look irrational from outside. In the prisoner's dilemma everyone could be better off, yet no one gains by moving alone. In games with moves in sequence, a Nash equilibrium can also rest on threats players would never carry out. A stricter idea, {{ref:nature-econ-734}}, removes these. The concept travels widely: in 1982 John Maynard Smith applied it to model the evolution of behavior.

nature-econ-729.title: Strategic dominance: a choice that is always better
nature-econ-729.text: Some choices are best no matter what anyone else does. One strategy dominates another if it always gives a better result, whatever the other players do. Strict dominance means always strictly better; weak dominance means never worse and sometimes better. A strategy that dominates every alternative is a dominant strategy, and rational players are usually assumed never to play a dominated one. The prisoner's dilemma is the classic case. Confessing dominates for each suspect, although both would do better staying silent. When every player has a strictly dominant strategy, the game has a single dominant-strategy equilibrium, and it need not be good for everyone. Strictly dominated strategies are never part of a Nash equilibrium, though weakly dominated ones can be.

nature-econ-680.title: Chicken: the game of who swerves first
nature-econ-680.text: Two drivers race toward each other. One must swerve or both may die, and the one who swerves is called a 'chicken'. Each driver does best by going straight while the other swerves, and a crash is the worst outcome for both. This is the game of Chicken, also called snowdrift: each player would like the other to back down, but the worst result is that neither does. It has three Nash equilibria. In two, the players choose opposite actions; in the third, each randomizes. That mixed equilibrium is the only symmetric one, and it is often worse for both than coordinating. Where the prisoner's dilemma is about the impossibility of cooperation, Chicken is about the inevitability of conflict. Repeated play can lead to turn-taking. The game even turns up at work as 'schedule chicken': project teams each promise unrealistic dates because no one wants to be first to admit delay.

nature-econ-700.title: Coordination games: the payoff of matching
nature-econ-700.text: Which side of the road should people drive on? Either works, as long as everyone picks the same one, and a shared standard saves lives if widely followed. That is a coordination game: a game played at the same time in which players earn more by choosing the same course of action. It has several Nash equilibria, each with players making matching choices, and each player's best move depends on what they expect the other to do. When it does not matter which option is picked as long as both pick the same, it is a pure coordination game. There is also a mixed equilibrium, but it is worse for both than either matching outcome and is not evolutionarily stable. Coordination games are closely tied to positive network externalities, the benefit of being in the same network as others. The {{ref:nature-econ-728}} is a coordination game where the best joint outcome needs trust, while a safer option needs none.

nature-econ-728.title: The stag hunt: a big prize that needs trust
nature-econ-728.text: Two hunters choose separately whether to chase a stag or a hare. A stag needs both of them; a hare can be caught alone but is worth far less. The problem goes back to Jean-Jacques Rousseau's Discourse on Inequality, and David Hume gave similar examples, such as two neighbours draining a meadow. The stag hunt, also called the assurance game or trust dilemma, has two pure equilibria. Hunting stag together pays most, while hunting hare alone is the safer, risk-dominant choice. Unlike the prisoner's dilemma, mutual cooperation is itself an equilibrium; what it needs is trust. That makes it a common analogy for social cooperation such as international climate agreements. Orcas that herd fish to the surface, a job needing many orcas, are an animal example. And expected punishment of defectors can turn a prisoner's dilemma into a stag hunt.

nature-econ-714.title: The extensive form: a game drawn as a tree
nature-econ-714.text: Some games unfold in turns, with each player seeing some of what came before. The extensive form draws such a game as a tree. It shows the order of moves, each player's choices at each point, what they know when they choose, and the payoffs at the end. It is a many-player version of a decision tree, and a fuller description than the payoff matrix of the normal form. The normal form generally suits simultaneous games; the extensive form suits sequential ones. Each end point, or leaf, lists one payoff for every player, and a play is a path from the root to a leaf. Chance events are modelled as moves by a fictitious player called Nature, whose branches carry probabilities. Such games are solved by {{ref:nature-econ-735}}, working from the end points back to the root. Harold W. Kuhn gave the general definition in 1953, extending one by von Neumann from 1928.

nature-econ-723.title: Repeated games: why meeting again changes everything
nature-econ-723.text: Two neighbouring petrol stations would both earn zero profit in a one-off price war. Yet they make profits, because they meet again every day. That is the logic of a repeated game: the same base game, called the stage game, played over and over by the same players. Repetition makes players weigh how today's action affects others' future actions, an effect sometimes called reputation. Whether the game repeats a fixed or an endless number of times matters greatly, leading to very different equilibria and best strategies. In the infinitely repeated prisoner's dilemma, the preferred strategy is to cooperate rather than play the one-shot Nash strategy. A game repeated an unknown number of times is treated the same way, since there is no known last round. Sustaining cooperation relies on punishing anyone who deviates. Results showing which outcomes can be sustained form the {{ref:nature-econ-717}}.

nature-econ-676.title: Bayesian games: playing with private information
nature-econ-676.text: A buyer bids for a used car whose quality only the owner knows. This market for lemons is a Bayesian game: a model of strategic decisions in which players have incomplete information, such as private knowledge of their own payoffs. John C. Harsanyi introduced such games in three papers in 1967 and 1968, and later shared the 1994 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences. His device was to let Nature assign each player a 'type' at the start, standing for the private information that player holds. Players hold a probability distribution over everyone's possible types; when no one has private information, it is called a common prior. Attaching probabilities to types let games of incomplete information be solved for the first time, and far more easily. It avoids endless 'I think that you think' reasoning by weighting all possible outcomes by probability at once.

nature-econ-737.title: Tit for tat: cooperate first, then copy
nature-econ-737.text: The phrase 'tit for tat', meaning equivalent retaliation, was first recorded in 1558. As a strategy for a repeated game, it is almost that simple: cooperate on the first move, then copy whatever the opponent did last. Anatol Rapoport entered it in Robert Axelrod's two tournaments around 1980, where it was both the simplest strategy and the most successful. Its success may help explain how animal and human groups came to live in mostly cooperative ways. In First World War trenches it appeared as the 'live and let live' system, an unspoken truce kept by matching retaliation. In repeated social dilemmas, cooperation may emerge when people adopt it. It has a weakness. A single misread move can trap two tit-for-tat players in an endless 'death spiral' of alternating retaliation. And in theory it is not a {{ref:nature-econ-734}} except under knife-edge conditions.

nature-econ-707.title: Evolutionary game theory: strategies that survive
nature-econ-707.text: Why do animals fight over resources in restrained, ritualized ways? That puzzle launched evolutionary game theory in 1973, when John Maynard Smith and George R. Price formally treated animal contests as strategies. The field uses game theory to study evolving populations, modelling Darwinian competition as a contest between strategies. Unlike classical game theory, it needs no rational players. It needs only inherited strategies whose success is tested by survival and reproduction. It focuses on how strategies change over time, which depends on how common each competing strategy is in the population. The fit is natural. Life's problems of getting food, surviving and reproducing resemble the economic problems of resource management, competitive strategy and investment. The approach has helped explain group selection, sexual selection, altruism, parental care, co-evolution and ecological dynamics.

nature-econ-694.title: Cooperative game theory: coalitions and binding deals
nature-econ-694.text: Some games allow binding deals. Cooperative game theory studies games in which groups of players can form coalitions and make agreements enforced from outside, for example by contract law. Non-cooperative games, by contrast, allow no alliances, or only agreements that enforce themselves, such as through threats a player would really carry out. The analysis asks which coalitions can form, what they can do jointly and what collective payoffs result. Its main assumption is that all players form one grand coalition. The question is then how to divide its total payoff. Researchers have proposed different answers, called solution concepts, such as the {{ref:nature-econ-706}} and the {{ref:nature-econ-726}}, each based on a different idea of fairness. The approach has even been proposed as a strategic theory of the firm, with different solutions mimicking different institutions.

nature-econ-732.title: Mixed strategies: the value of being unpredictable
nature-econ-732.text: A soccer penalty kick has no stable fixed plan for either side, so kicker and goalie should both randomize their direction. That is a mixed strategy: choosing among pure strategies at random with set probabilities, rather than committing to one plan. A pure strategy is a fully fixed plan, and it counts as a mixed strategy that picks one option with probability 1. Mixing helps where no pure strategy is a best response, keeping a player unpredictable, and payoffs then become expected payoffs. Not every finite game has a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium, as matching pennies shows, but every one has an equilibrium once mixing is allowed. Critics in the 1980s found mixed strategies intuitively problematic. Harsanyi's purification reads them as our ignorance of players' private information, and another view treats them as the shares of a large group of players using each option.

nature-econ-735.title: Backward induction: solving a game from the end
nature-econ-735.text: To solve a game played in turns, start at the end. Backward induction works out what the final mover would do, then reasons back step by step to the start. At each step it removes branches where a player would make a move that is not in their interest at that point. Tic-tac-toe has a well-known backward-induction solution, and in theory even Go has one. Finite repeated games can be solved this way. Games repeated forever, or an unknown number of times, cannot, because there is no last round to start from. Kaminski (2019) proved that a generalized backward induction finds all of the {{ref:nature-econ-734}} outcomes in a broad class of games.

nature-econ-734.title: Subgame perfect equilibrium: ruling out empty threats
nature-econ-734.text: Reinhard Selten proposed a sharper version of the Nash equilibrium in 1965. A subgame perfect equilibrium, for games with moves in sequence, requires the strategies to form a Nash equilibrium in every subgame, from any point onward. This rules out non-credible threats, ones a player would not actually want to carry out, so strategies stay rational throughout the game. Every finite game with complete information and perfect recall, where players remember all past actions, has one. In finite games it is usually found by backward induction, though that does not work for infinite games or games with hidden moves. The ultimatum game is a classic example with fewer subgame perfect equilibria than Nash equilibria. In a finitely repeated prisoner's dilemma, backward induction makes both players defect in every round. Yet firms in repeated Cournot competition can collude on the monopoly outcome in a subgame perfect equilibrium, if they are patient enough.

nature-econ-717.title: The folk theorem: patience makes almost anything possible
nature-econ-717.text: Game theorists widely knew this result in the 1950s, yet nobody had published it, which is how it got its name. The folk theorem is a family of results showing that repeated games have a great many equilibrium outcomes. Almost any payoff can be sustained if players are patient enough. The phrase 'almost any' means every payoff that is feasible and individually rational, that is, better than what each player can guarantee alone. The simplest proof uses a harsh rule called grim trigger: cooperate until someone deviates, then punish them forever. Friedman's 1971 version strengthened it to subgame-perfect equilibria, where punishment threats must be credible. The result explains why agreements between countries are kept without enforcement, since relations are long-term, though an impatient country is hard to punish credibly. In a close-knit group it shows how traditions and taboos can be upheld by social norms. Franklin Fisher noted its limit: it does not predict what firms will do, only that cost and demand alone cannot explain oligopoly.

nature-econ-708.title: Evolutionarily stable strategies: holding off invaders
nature-econ-708.text: A strategy that succeeds in nature must be able to spread when rare and to hold its ground once common. An evolutionarily stable strategy passes the second test. Once common in a large population, it cannot be invaded by any rare mutant strategy. It is akin to the Nash equilibrium of classical game theory, but with stricter mathematical conditions. In the {{ref:nature-econ-681}}, the stable strategy is a mixed one. Not every game has such a strategy. The rock-paper-scissors game played by male side-blotched lizards has none, only endless cycles around a Nash equilibrium.
